mcqs.question: A stakeholder says they need "real-time" data. What's the most useful next question to ask?
options: Which streaming framework do you want us to use?
Would you prefer Kafka or Kinesis?
How much budget is available for infrastructure?
What concrete business consequence happens if this data is instead an hour late, or a minute late?
mcqs.explanation: Grounding the request in a specific consequence at different latencies reveals the actual requirement — most "real-time" requests turn out to tolerate minutes just fine once pressed on what breaks. Jumping straight to tool or framework choice skips the step that determines whether streaming is even needed.

mcqs.question: Which statement accurately compares micro-batch and continuous streaming architectures?
options: Micro-batch always has lower latency than continuous streaming
Continuous streaming has no operational cost advantage or disadvantage compared to micro-batch
Micro-batch keeps a batch-style failure model (a run either succeeds or fails cleanly) while continuous streaming must handle failures while data keeps arriving
Continuous streaming cannot be implemented using Kafka or Flink
mcqs.explanation: Micro-batch retains the simpler batch semantics of discrete, retriable runs, while continuous streaming must manage offset tracking, backpressure, and checkpointing continuously — a genuinely higher operational bar. Continuous streaming typically has lower latency but higher operational cost than micro-batch, and Kafka/Flink are exactly the tools used to build it.

mcqs.question: Why does the guide recommend trying micro-batch before reaching for continuous, event-by-event streaming?
options: Micro-batch is always faster than continuous streaming in every scenario
Continuous streaming is deprecated technology that vendors no longer support
Micro-batch delivers freshness that feels real-time for most use cases while keeping simpler, batch-style operational and failure semantics
Micro-batch requires no orchestration or scheduling infrastructure at all
mcqs.explanation: Sub-minute freshness with the simpler failure model of discrete batch runs satisfies the vast majority of "real-time-ish" needs without taking on continuous streaming's operational complexity, which is why it's the pragmatic default to try first. Continuous streaming is still an actively used, non-deprecated approach, it's faster in absolute latency terms, and micro-batch still needs scheduling infrastructure, just less frequently exercised.

mcqs.question: A team builds a Kafka streaming pipeline for a dashboard that only ever needed nightly refreshes, mainly because streaming seemed more impressive to build. What check would have caught this before the build started?
options: Naming the specific decision or action that becomes possible with lower latency, and confirming someone would actually act on it within that window
Checking whether Kafka is compatible with the team's existing cloud provider
Estimating the exact throughput in messages per second the pipeline would need to handle
Reviewing whether any competitor uses a similar streaming architecture
mcqs.explanation: If no one's workflow or decision actually changes because the data arrives faster, the latency reduction has no real value, which is the check that exposes speculative streaming builds before they're started. Cloud compatibility and throughput estimates are useful once you've already decided streaming is warranted, and competitor architecture says nothing about your own latency requirement.

mcqs.question: Why does a nightly batch job fail structurally, not just slowly, as a fraud-detection approach?
options: Batch jobs cannot run machine learning models at all
By the time a nightly job flags a fraudulent transaction, the funds have typically already moved, so faster batch scheduling alone can't fix it
Batch jobs are more expensive to run than streaming jobs at any scale
Nightly batch jobs cannot process transaction data in any format
mcqs.explanation: The failure is structural: the fraud has already completed and funds moved by the time a next-day batch job even runs, so the problem isn't merely "too slow," it's that the decision window has already closed — only real-time scoring, before the transaction completes, can act in time. Batch jobs can run ML models and process transaction data fine, and streaming is typically the more, not less, expensive approach operationally.
